# Golden backup fixtures

One encrypted backup per schema version, kept so that the day somebody restores a phone they lost a
year ago is not the day we find out old backups stopped opening (006 T028).

| File | Schema | Written by | Recovery key |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `schema-v1.obalka` | 1 | `c747297` — the last commit before `BACKUP_SCHEMA_VERSION` moved to 2, in the history **before this repository was published** | `TEST0N1YF1XTVREKEY00` |

## Why the bytes were not generated by today's code

Because that would prove nothing. `compatibility.test.ts` already fingerprints the schema, and every
migration ever written passes it — it compares today's shape against today's recorded shape, which is
two pieces of the same build agreeing with each other. The question is whether a file written a year
ago still opens, and only a file actually written a year ago can answer it.

So `scripts/make-backup-fixture.mjs` checks the old commit out into a git worktree, runs the app's own
payload writer and envelope there, and brings the bytes back:

```sh
node scripts/make-backup-fixture.mjs --ref c907ea5^ --version 1
```

That ref is not in this repository. The public history starts from a single commit, and `c907ea5^`
belongs to the development history before it — so version 1 cannot be regenerated from here, and the
committed bytes are the artifact. The command is kept because it is the honest record of how they were
made, and because the same script is how version 2 onwards gets a fixture, from commits that ARE here.

The script refuses if the ref's `BACKUP_SCHEMA_VERSION` is not the version asked for, which is the one
mistake that would quietly make the whole exercise pointless.

## The key is in the repository on purpose

`TEST0N1YF1XTVREKEY00` protects nothing. Everything inside the fixture is invented — two boxes
that do not exist, four messages nobody sent, one draft and one reminder about them — and a golden
test that cannot open its own golden file is decoration. Nothing in here is government mail
(Constitution III), and nothing came off a real box (Constitution VII).

It is spelled the way it is so that if it ever turns up in a log or a support bundle it reads as what
it is: `TEST 0N1Y F1XTVRE KEY`.

It is written **ungrouped** everywhere — here and in both TypeScript files — and rebuilt with the
app's own `format()` at the point of use. The secret scanner has a rule for a grouped recovery key
(`.trivy-secret.yaml`), and it is right to have one; the alternative to one function call was three
entries in `.trivyignore.yaml`, permanently exempting the files most likely to pick up a real key by
accident later. The string that reaches `seal()` is identical either way.

## Argon2id is deliberately cheap here

The fixture was sealed at `m = 8192, t = 1` against the `KDF_DEFAULTS` of `m = 65536, t = 3`. Real
backups are still written at the defaults. Two reasons, and the second is the better one:

1. The golden test opens this file on every run, and a second of pure-JavaScript Argon2id per run is
   a second people eventually spend removing the test.
2. The parameters travel **inside** the envelope header. A file made at 8 MiB opening on a build that
   writes 64 MiB is exactly the property that lets the costs be raised as phones get faster without
   orphaning every backup already written — and nothing else in the suite exercises it, because
   everything else seals and opens in the same breath.

## When the schema moves again

Add the new fixture; do not replace this one. A version 1 backup does not stop existing because a
version 3 shipped, and the chain has to carry it the whole way.

```sh
node scripts/make-backup-fixture.mjs --ref <last commit at version 2> --version 2
```

Then add a `describe` block for it in `goldenRestore.test.ts`. If the old version's `BackupSource`
no longer matches `scripts/fixtures/writeFixture.test.ts`, amend that file for the new shape — git
still holds the version the old worktree needs.
